brief.situation: You are the on-call solutions architect for Tidewater Tickets, a fictional ticket seller. At 10:00 login errors spike and the site slows. A major concert goes on sale at 11:00. The site runs CloudFront in front of an Application Load Balancer, an Auto Scaling group of 6 instances and an RDS orders database.
handover: No AWS WAF web ACL is set up yet. AWS Shield Standard is on, as it is for every AWS account.
The ALB's security group allows HTTPS from anywhere.
howItWorks: The board shows the distribution, the origin, the database and the business, with what is set up in each.
Each task takes your time: start it, then let the work finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes. The attackers keep working on the same clock.
When you close the incident, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the record: what the two attacks were, which AWS controls stopped each and why those, and what still has to change.

parts.label: Two attacks
parts.criteria: Separates the layer 7 login flood (many addresses, each far above a customer's rate) from the SQL injection probes on /search, from metrics and logs.
parts.modelAnswer: Metrics showed a login flood from about 2,000 addresses at layer 7, with network-layer traffic normal; the logs showed each address at about 600 requests per 5 minutes against under 20 for customers, and three addresses sending UNION SELECT probes to /search.

parts.label: Controls
parts.criteria: AWS WAF on CloudFront: the managed SQL database rule group, a rate-based rule set between customer and attacker rates, and the ALB admitting only the CloudFront prefix list; explains why Shield Standard and security groups do not stop this.
parts.modelAnswer: Shield Standard covers network and transport layer attacks, not an HTTP flood that looks like logins, and security groups have no deny rules. A web ACL on the distribution with the SQL database rule group blocked the probes, a 300-per-5-minutes rule on /login stopped the flood without blocking the university's shared address, and restricting the ALB to the CloudFront origin-facing prefix list stopped the botnet going around the web ACL.

parts.label: Still to do
parts.criteria: The injectable query must be fixed in code (parameterized statements); WAF is defense in depth. Mentions logging or tuning the rules.
parts.modelAnswer: The search query is still injectable; the WAF rule only filters known patterns. The developers parameterize it this week, and we keep WAF logging on to tune the rate limit before the next on-sale.

expertPath.text: Metrics: a layer 7 flood on /login. Logs: flood addresses at about 600 requests per 5 minutes, customers under 20, and SQL injection probes on /search.
A web ACL on the CloudFront distribution; the managed SQL database rule group, Block; a rate-based rule on /login at 300 per 5 minutes per IP.
The ALB security group admits only the CloudFront origin-facing prefix list, so nothing goes around the web ACL. Record: fix the query in code.

protected.headline: Good: both attacks stopped at the edge
protected.body: You read the evidence, matched each attack to the AWS WAF control that stops it, set the rate limit between the attacker's rate and your customers', and closed the path around CloudFront.

protectedGaps.headline: Stopped, with gaps
protectedGaps.body: Both attacks are stopped. The criteria show where customers were blocked, the web ACL was bypassed, or the record went wrong.

dataStolen.headline: The data got out
dataStolen.body: The probes were in the logs from the start. A managed SQL database rule group on a web ACL takes minutes; the flood was louder but the injection was the bigger risk.

takenDown.headline: Too blunt
takenDown.body: Taking the site offline does what the attacker wanted. AWS WAF can block both attacks while customers keep buying.

onsaleDown.headline: The flood came back
onsaleDown.body: A web ACL only filters what passes through CloudFront. With the load balancer open to the internet, the botnet went around it; the CloudFront prefix list closes that path.

stillOpen.headline: Left open
stillOpen.body: One attack still had a way in when the case closed. Shield Standard covers network and transport layer floods only, and security groups cannot deny.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Metrics show a layer 7 flood on /login from about 2,000 addresses, with network and transport layer traffic normal, so Shield Standard (already on) is not what stops it. The logs show each flood address at about 600 requests per 5 minutes, customers under 20 and a university's shared address about 80, plus SQL injection probes on /search. Associate a web ACL with the CloudFront distribution, add the AWS managed SQL database rule group with Block, and a rate-based rule on /login at 300 per 5 minutes per IP (10 would block real customers, 2,000 blocks nothing). Restrict the ALB's security group to the CloudFront origin-facing prefix list so the botnet cannot go around the web ACL. Security groups have no deny rules, and scaling out only feeds the flood. The query itself must still be parameterized.
